title: Every weight gets its own ruler
allegory: Adam is like handing every weight its own ruler: it keeps a running average of each weight's slope and of how big that slope usually is, then measures the slope in its own ruler's units, so busy and quiet weights both take sensible steps.
map: the running sense of which way is downhill
m: a moving average of the gradient, which is momentum
each weight's own ruler: how big its slopes usually are
√v: the root of a moving average of the squared gradient, as in RMSprop
reading the slope in the ruler's units
a new ruler starts blank, so early readings get topped up
bias correction: divide by (1 - βᵗ), because m and v start at zero
jumpy slopes stretch the ruler, so those weights step carefully
noisy gradients inflate √v and shrink the step
credit: The 'momentum plus RMSprop' framing follows Andrew Ng, Deep Learning Specialization, course 2 (Improving Deep Neural Networks), 'Adam optimization algorithm'.
where_else: AdamW, the default optimiser for every transformer you train in later chapters
Momentum and RMSprop, Adam's two halves, each still used on its own
Running averages elsewhere: BatchNorm keeps the same kind of slowly updated statistics

hamming.what: An optimiser that steps each weight by its averaged gradient divided by the root of its averaged squared gradient.
hamming.when: Almost every time you train a network in this course, usually in its AdamW form.
hamming.why: Dividing by each weight's own typical gradient size gives every parameter a sensible step at once, where a single learning rate is too big for some weights and too small for others.
